doc.title: Herb Ellis interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Charlie Christian's influence and his early death
summary: Hearing Charlie Christian made Ellis play far fewer notes; Christian changed solo guitar and died at 23, as did bassist Jimmy Blanton at 21.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Now you say that Charlie Christian was one of your influences.
Explain his influence and then talk about how the jazz guitar has evolved from that time.

Well Charlie Christian, I mean when I first heard him I was just absolutely stunned you know. And I was a kid at that time and I could play a lot of notes, I mean a lot of notes, but they were worthless you know. So when I heard him and it got to me so then I started playing from playing a million notes to playing almost no notes. I mean each note had to be sent to me directly from heaven before I would consider playing it. And somewhere in there I’ve struck a happy medium. And Charlie changed the whole nature of the guitar. He played it sort of the way people have played guitaristic, sort of unlike that. Because he played more like a tenor saxophone would play you know. And he changed the whole course of solo guitaring. And you know that he died when he was 23. Yep. He could still be living and playing.
That’s another theme in jazz is the early and tragic death of some of its greatest players.
Yeah well that’s true. He had tuberculosis. And Jimmy Blanton died when he was 21, the bassist with Duke Ellington.
